questions.stem: What is « le verlan »?
options: A formal register used in official documents
An old spelling system replaced in the 1990s
A slang formed by reversing the syllables of words
A regional accent of southern France
questions.explanation: « Verlan » is itself verlan — « l'envers » (the reverse) with its syllables swapped. « Meuf » from « femme » and « ouf » from « fou » are the standard examples, and several have entered ordinary speech.

questions.stem: What is the Académie française?
options: A university in Paris for foreign students
The government department that runs French schools
A body that advises on the French language and its usage
The French national school examination board
questions.explanation: Founded in 1635, the Académie publishes a dictionary and recommends usage. Its rulings carry prestige rather than legal force, and speakers regularly ignore them — which is itself worth noticing.

questions.stem: Which country has the largest French-speaking population?
options: The Democratic Republic of the Congo
France
Canada
Belgium
questions.explanation: The DRC has more French speakers than France. The centre of gravity of the language has moved to Africa, and population growth is widening the gap.

questions.stem: What does it mean that a French word is 'borrowed' into English?
options: It can be used only in formal English
It has the opposite meaning in the two languages
It was invented by English speakers to sound French
English adopted it from French and kept it in use
questions.explanation: The Norman conquest of 1066 began centuries of borrowing, which is why English has both 'cow' (Germanic, the animal) and 'beef' (from « bœuf », the meat) — the farmer and the diner spoke different languages.

questions.stem: Why does French distinguish « tu » and « vous » when English does not?
options: English lost its own equivalent distinction over time
French added the distinction only in the twentieth century
English never had a second-person pronoun system
The distinction exists only in written French
questions.explanation: English once had 'thou' for the familiar singular and 'you' for the formal or plural. 'Thou' fell out of use, leaving one form to do both jobs — so this is a gap in English rather than an extra rule in French.

questions.stem: What does « tutoyer » mean?
options: To greet someone formally
To address someone using « tu »
To speak very quickly
To translate between two languages
questions.explanation: « Tutoyer » and « vouvoyer » are verbs for the act of choosing a pronoun — a sign of how socially loaded the choice is. English has no verb for it because it has no choice to make.

questions.stem: Why is register a grammatical matter in French rather than only a matter of vocabulary?
options: Informal French has no verb tenses
Register affects only written French
Formality changes pronouns, verb forms and question structure
Formal French uses a different alphabet
questions.explanation: Moving from « Tu viens ? » to « Est-ce que vous venez ? » to « Venez-vous ? » changes the pronoun and the whole question structure. English adjusts mostly through word choice and tone instead.

questions.stem: What is « l'argot »?
options: Slang or informal vocabulary
A regional dialect of Brittany
The formal language of the courts
A written accent mark
questions.explanation: « L'argot » is slang. Knowing it exists matters for comprehension, since film and song lean on it heavily, while written schoolwork is expected in standard French.

questions.stem: Which is an example of French used as a shared language between speakers of other languages?
options: French lessons in an Australian secondary school
A French novel translated into English
Government and schooling across much of West Africa
Conversation between two families in rural France
questions.explanation: In many African states French serves as a common administrative language between communities with different first languages. That role — a lingua franca — is different from being anyone's mother tongue.

questions.stem: Why do Quebec French and European French differ in vocabulary?
options: Quebec French borrows only from Indigenous languages
The Académie française assigns different words to each
They developed separately after centuries of limited contact
Quebec French is an older form that never changed
questions.explanation: Separation plus different neighbouring languages produces divergence, exactly as it did for Australian and British English. Quebec resists English borrowings more strongly, so « courriel » is used where France often says « email ».

questions.stem: What does « la laïcité » refer to in France?
options: The right to free secondary education
The protection of the French language by law
The separation of religion from the state
The system of regional government
questions.explanation: « Laïcité » was established in law in 1905 and shapes public debate about schools and public life. It has no exact English equivalent, which is why the French word is used in English writing about France.

questions.stem: Which statement about accents in French is accurate?
options: They indicate which syllable is stressed
They can change both pronunciation and meaning
They are decorative and can be omitted in writing
They appear only on capital letters
questions.explanation: « Ou » means or and « où » means where; « a » is has and « à » is to. Dropping an accent can change the word, so it is a spelling error rather than a stylistic choice.

questions.stem: Why might a French speaker consider « Je veux un café » impolite?
options: It places the object before the verb
It uses an informal pronoun with a stranger
It uses a direct present tense where the conditional is expected
It uses the wrong gender for « café »
questions.explanation: Politeness in French is carried by the verb form: « je voudrais » signals the request as softened. The sentence is grammatically perfect, which is exactly why grammar alone will not tell you it lands badly.

questions.stem: What does the existence of « courriel » alongside « email » show about language?
options: Technical terms are always translated by law
Older words always displace newer borrowings
Communities can consciously shape their own vocabulary
French has no way to borrow words from other languages
questions.explanation: « Courriel » was coined in Quebec from « courrier électronique » and is widely used there while France often keeps « email ». Two communities made different choices about the same borrowing.

questions.stem: Why is understanding cultural context necessary for interpreting a French text, not just vocabulary?
options: Meaning depends on assumptions and references a reader may not share
French grammar changes according to the region
French texts rarely state their subject directly
Vocabulary alone cannot be looked up in a dictionary
questions.explanation: A reference to « la rentrée » or « le bac » carries weight for a French reader that a dictionary entry does not convey. This is what UL04 means by identity shaping ways of communicating.

questions.stem: What does the pair « cow » and « beef » in English reveal about its history?
options: One word is a regional variant of the other
Anglo-Saxon and Norman French words survived side by side
English invented two words for every farm animal
The words were borrowed from French at the same time
questions.explanation: The animal keeps its Old English name and the meat takes the Norman French one — « bœuf ». The same pattern gives sheep/mutton and pig/pork, and it records who farmed and who dined after 1066.

questions.stem: Why does French have gendered nouns for objects while English does not?
options: French kept a grammatical system that English gradually lost
French assigns gender based on the qualities of each object
Gender was introduced by the Académie française
English never inherited gender from any earlier language
questions.explanation: Old English had grammatical gender and lost it; French inherited and kept the Latin system. Gender carries no meaning about the object — « la table » is feminine for no recoverable reason.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say French is a pluricentric language?
options: It has more than one writing system
It has both a formal and an informal register
It has several recognised standard forms in different countries
It is spoken on more than one continent
questions.explanation: France, Quebec, Belgium and Switzerland each have accepted standards, with their own vocabulary and usage. English is pluricentric in the same way, which is why Australian English is not simply incorrect British.

questions.stem: What does it mean that a language has 'register'?
options: It has a fixed written form
It records new words each year
It is spoken in more than one country
It has levels of formality for the same idea
questions.explanation: « Je veux », « je voudrais » and « auriez-vous » all ask for the same thing at three different levels.

questions.stem: Which is the most formal way to ask 'do you have a room'?
options: Auriez-vous une chambre ?
Vous avez une chambre ?
T'as une chambre ?
Une chambre ?
questions.explanation: The conditional plus inversion is the top of the register scale. Dropping to « t'as » with a receptionist would be startling.

questions.stem: What does dropping the « ne » in « je sais pas » signal?
options: Incorrect French
A regional dialect
A question rather than a statement
Informal spoken French
questions.explanation: Spoken French drops the « ne » constantly; written French keeps it. It is a register marker, not an error.

questions.stem: Why is « nous » often replaced by « on » in conversation?
options: Nous is only used in writing about the past
It is shorter and takes a simpler verb form
Nous is considered rude
On is more formal
questions.explanation: « On y va » against « nous y allons ». Written French still prefers « nous ».

questions.stem: What is « le franglais »?
options: A dialect of northern France
Old French
French mixed with English borrowings
French spoken in England
questions.explanation: The term is often used critically, but borrowing has run in both directions for a thousand years.

questions.stem: Why did Quebec coin « courriel » for email?
options: Because email is hard to pronounce
To resist an English borrowing
Because email was invented there
Because France asked them to
questions.explanation: Quebec's language policy is more protective than France's, which is why Quebec French often has a home-grown word where France uses the English.

questions.stem: What does Quebec say instead of « le week-end »?
options: Le samedi
Les jours libres
La fin de semaine
Le repos
questions.explanation: France borrowed the English word; Quebec built one from French parts. The same divide shows up in « courriel » and « stationnement ».

questions.stem: Which is a Quebec word for a car park?
options: Parking
Garage
Arret
Stationnement
questions.explanation: France uses « le parking », borrowed from English. Quebec uses a French formation.

questions.stem: Why do some French words have no exact English equivalent?
options: English avoids borrowing
Languages divide meaning differently
English has fewer words
French words are always longer
questions.explanation: « Depaysement » and « flaner » each need a phrase in English. The same is true in reverse for English words like 'serendipity'.

questions.stem: What does « depaysement » describe?
options: Homesickness
Leaving a country permanently
Loss of citizenship
The feeling of being somewhere unfamiliar
questions.explanation: It can be pleasant or unsettling. English needs a whole clause to carry it.

questions.stem: What does « flaner » mean?
options: To hurry
To complain
To rest
To wander without purpose
questions.explanation: The « flaneur » who strolls the city observing is a figure in French literature, which is why the word carries more than 'to stroll'.

questions.stem: Why is literal translation often inadequate?
options: Grammar is identical between languages
Dictionaries are incomplete
Idioms and connotation do not transfer word for word
Words have different lengths
questions.explanation: « Il pleut des cordes » is 'it is raining ropes'. Translating the words gives the wrong register and the wrong image.

questions.stem: What does « avoir le cafard » mean?
options: To be lucky
To be in a hurry
To feel low
To have a cold
questions.explanation: Literally 'to have the cockroach'. Idioms rarely survive a word-for-word crossing.

questions.stem: What does « poser un lapin » mean?
options: To stand someone up
To ask a question
To make a mistake
To buy a gift
questions.explanation: Literally 'to place a rabbit'. Knowing every word in the phrase gets you nowhere near the meaning.

questions.stem: What is « le verlan » built on?
options: Reversing the syllables of a word
Adding suffixes
Borrowing from English
Shortening long words
questions.explanation: « L'envers » becomes « verlan » by its own rule. « Femme » becomes « meuf » and « arabe » becomes « beur ».

questions.stem: Which word is verlan for « fete »?
options: Teuf
Feut
Etfe
Fete-la
questions.explanation: The syllables swap. Some verlan words have become so common that they are now in dictionaries.

questions.stem: Why does slang change faster than standard language?
options: It marks group identity, so it renews as it spreads
It follows no grammatical rules of any kind
It is spoken only and never written anywhere
It is invented by dictionary editors each year
questions.explanation: Once outsiders adopt a term it stops marking the group, so the group moves on. Verlan has been re-verlanised for this reason.

questions.stem: What does it mean that French is an official language of the UN?
options: It is the only language used
It is used only in Europe
It replaced English in 1945
It is one of six working languages there
questions.explanation: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. It is one reason French remains a diplomatic language.

questions.stem: Why is French used at the Olympic Games?
options: France hosts the most Games
It is the language of sport
It was chosen by a vote in 1980
The modern Games were founded by a Frenchman
questions.explanation: Pierre de Coubertin founded the modern movement, and French remains a first official language of the IOC alongside English.

questions.stem: What does « la laicite » mean in French public life?
options: Equality before the law
The separation of religion and the state
Freedom of the press
Compulsory schooling
questions.explanation: It dates from a 1905 law and shapes debates about religious dress in schools in ways that differ sharply from Australia.

questions.stem: Why might a French text need cultural knowledge as well as vocabulary?
options: French texts are longer than their translations
French has more synonyms than English does
References and assumptions are not in the dictionary
French grammar is too irregular to read reliably
questions.explanation: A mention of « la rentree » or « le bac » assumes you know what they are and what they feel like.

questions.stem: What does « le bac » refer to?
options: The school-leaving examination
A university degree
A public holiday
A type of transport
questions.explanation: Short for « le baccalaureat ». Results day is a national news event in France.

questions.stem: What does the borrowing of « rendezvous » into English show?
options: The word was invented in England
English takes words it lacks a term for
French has no word for meeting
English cannot form compounds
questions.explanation: English has 'meeting' and borrowed « rendezvous » for the shade of meaning it did not have.

questions.stem: Which English word arrived through French after the Norman Conquest?
options: House
Water
Hand
Government
questions.explanation: Law, government and cuisine vocabulary came through French; the basic words of daily life stayed Germanic.

questions.stem: What does the pair 'ask' and 'enquire' show about English?
options: It has Germanic and French-derived synonyms
One of them is incorrect
They mean exactly the same thing
Both came from French
questions.explanation: The Germanic word is usually plainer and the French-derived one more formal, which gives English its register range.

questions.stem: Why does French have an official language authority when English does not?
options: French changes faster
English has no dictionaries
French is spoken in fewer countries
France has a tradition of state involvement in language
questions.explanation: The Academie francaise dates from 1635. English standardisation came through printers and dictionaries rather than the state.

questions.stem: Can the Academie francaise force anyone to use its recommendations?
options: Yes, in broadcasting only
No, its authority is advisory
Yes, in all publications
Yes, in schools only
questions.explanation: Its recommendations carry prestige rather than legal force, and speakers routinely ignore them.

questions.stem: What is an accent, in the sense of how someone sounds?
options: A regional or social way of pronouncing a language
A written mark placed above a vowel letter
A grammatical error made by a second-language speaker
A separate language spoken alongside the standard
questions.explanation: The word does double duty in English. In French the written mark is also « un accent », which is a useful coincidence to notice.

questions.stem: Which statement about accents is accurate?
options: Standard French has no accent
Accents disappear in writing
Everyone speaks with an accent
Only regional speakers have accents
questions.explanation: There is no accentless way to speak. What gets called 'no accent' is usually just the prestige variety.

questions.stem: Why do southern French accents pronounce more final consonants?
options: It is a recent change
Southern speakers read more
It is taught in schools there
Regional varieties preserve different features
questions.explanation: Regional varieties are not degraded standard French; they have their own histories and their own consistency.

questions.stem: What does 'language contact' mean?
options: Teaching two languages in the same classroom
Writing one language in another's alphabet
Languages influencing each other where speakers meet
Translating a document from one language to another
questions.explanation: Contact produces borrowing, new varieties and sometimes new languages entirely. English and French are a long-running example.

questions.stem: What is a creole language?
options: A regional dialect of French spoken in the Caribbean
An artificial language designed for trade
A language that borrows without any grammar of its own
A full language that developed from a contact variety
questions.explanation: Haitian Creole draws much vocabulary from French and has its own grammar and its own native speakers.

questions.stem: Where is Haitian Creole spoken alongside French?
options: Morocco
Belgium
Senegal
Haiti
questions.explanation: Both are official in Haiti, though Creole is the everyday language of almost everyone.

questions.stem: Why do some countries keep a colonial language as official?
options: It was required by treaty
It is easier to learn
It is neutral between local language groups
Local languages have no writing
questions.explanation: Choosing one local language over others can be politically fraught, which is one reason several African states kept French.

questions.stem: What does it mean that French is a lingua franca in parts of Africa?
options: It lets speakers of different first languages communicate
It is the first language of almost everyone there
It is used in written documents and nowhere else
It has replaced the local languages entirely
questions.explanation: Most speakers there use it alongside one or more African languages rather than instead of them.

questions.stem: Why does the centre of gravity of French speakers keep shifting to Africa?
options: France is losing speakers
French is no longer taught in Europe
African French is a separate language
Population growth is faster there
questions.explanation: Demographic projections put most future French speakers in Africa, which will shape how the language changes.

questions.stem: What does 'code-switching' describe?
options: Learning two languages at once
Using slang with friends
Moving between languages within a conversation
Translating a written text
questions.explanation: Bilingual speakers switch for precision, for identity or because one language simply has the better word to hand.

questions.stem: Why is code-switching not a sign of poor language skills?
options: It follows no pattern
It replaces grammar with gesture
It requires fluent control of both systems
It only happens in writing
questions.explanation: Switching at the right points takes command of the grammar of both languages, which is why monolinguals cannot do it.

questions.stem: What does « tu » signal that English cannot mark grammatically?
options: How many people are being addressed at once
Which tense the following verb will take
The gender of the person doing the speaking
Closeness or familiarity with the person addressed
questions.explanation: English lost « thou » and now signals this through names, tone and word choice instead of the pronoun.

questions.stem: Why does using « tu » wrongly matter more than a grammar slip?
options: It carries a social judgement about the relationship
It changes the meaning of the verb
It is grammatically impossible
It marks the sentence as a question
questions.explanation: A verb-ending error reads as a learner's mistake; the wrong pronoun reads as a claim about how well you know someone.

questions.stem: What does « on » let a speaker avoid?
options: Using the past tense
Making the sentence negative
Naming who did something
Using a verb
questions.explanation: « On a ferme la route » says the road was closed without saying by whom, which is useful and sometimes evasive.

questions.stem: Why do languages borrow food words so readily?
options: The food and its name arrive together
Food words are shorter
They have no grammar
They are easier to pronounce
questions.explanation: Croissant, sushi and pizza travelled with the thing itself. There was no existing word waiting for them.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a borrowed word has been 'naturalised'?
options: It was translated
It kept its original spelling
It follows the host language's rules
It is no longer used
questions.explanation: English pluralises 'cafes' with an s rather than following French. Once that happens the word behaves as English.

questions.stem: Why does French spell « le football » as one borrowed word?
options: It was taken whole from English
It was invented in France
It is a translation
It follows Latin rules
questions.explanation: France took the word and the game. Quebec more often uses « le soccer », borrowed from North American English instead.

questions.stem: What does a language's word for a new technology usually depend on?
options: The alphabet used
The number of speakers
Where the technology arrives from
How long the word is
questions.explanation: « Ordinateur » was coined in French; « le smartphone » was borrowed. The route decides.

questions.stem: Why was « ordinateur » coined rather than borrowing 'computer'?
options: The machine was invented in France
English had no word for it
French deliberately built a term from its own roots
Computer was already taken
questions.explanation: IBM France asked a professor for a French word in 1955. It stuck, which borrowed terms often do not.

questions.stem: Which statement about gendered job titles in French is accurate?
options: Job titles never take gender
Feminine forms are banned in Quebec
Feminine forms have been increasingly adopted
All job titles are masculine by law
questions.explanation: « Une autrice », « une professeure » and « une ecrivaine » are now widely used, and Quebec moved earlier than France.

questions.stem: Why does a language's grammar sometimes become a political question?
options: Grammar choices can carry social claims
Grammar is set by parliament
Grammar changes every year
Grammar has no effect on meaning
questions.explanation: Debates over feminised job titles and inclusive writing are arguments about who the language treats as visible.

questions.stem: What does « vouvoyer » a colleague suggest in a French workplace?
options: The colleague is senior
A professional distance is being kept
The colleague is disliked
The speaker is foreign
questions.explanation: Some workplaces are on « tu » throughout and others firmly on « vous ». Reading which is a practical skill.

questions.stem: Why is an interpreter's job harder than a dictionary suggests?
options: There are too many words
Speech is faster than writing
Dictionaries are out of date
Register, idiom and intent all have to cross
questions.explanation: Getting the words right and the register wrong can change a polite request into a demand.

questions.stem: What does subtitling lose compared with the original?
options: Some nuance, because subtitles must be brief
All of the meaning of the original dialogue
The order in which events are shown
The names of the characters who are speaking
questions.explanation: Reading speed caps how much text can be on screen, so subtitles compress. Dubbing loses the original performance instead.

questions.stem: Why do some French films keep their titles untranslated abroad?
options: Translating a film title is not legally permitted
Film titles are impossible to translate at all
Leaving the title alone costs the distributor less
The title carries a tone translation would lose
questions.explanation: « Amelie » travelled under a shortened French title. Sometimes the foreignness is part of what is being sold.

questions.stem: What does learning a second language tend to reveal about the first?
options: That vocabulary is fixed
Choices you had not noticed you were making
That the first language is simpler
That grammar is universal
questions.explanation: Meeting gendered nouns or a tu/vous split makes you notice what English does and does not mark.

questions.stem: Why is « faux ami » a useful term to know?
options: It is the French word for friend
It describes slang
It refers to a translation tool
It names a predictable kind of error
questions.explanation: Knowing the category makes you check « librairie » and « actuellement » rather than trusting the resemblance.

questions.stem: What does the variety of French across the world suggest about languages generally?
options: They merge into one another
They change as communities use them
They are fixed by dictionaries
They become simpler over time
questions.explanation: Variation is the normal state. A single unchanging standard is the exception that has to be actively maintained.
